newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Jervois eyes big buyer for scandium metal.
newsitem.headline: Jervois eyes big buyer for scandium metal.

text.p: Jervois Mining NL, which is exploring for the rare metal scandium in Australia, said on Tuesday it may have a ready overseas buyer for the metal.

Jervois Managing Director Duncan Pursell said the company had been advised by Ashurst Technology Ltd of Baltimore, Maryland, that it was interested in obtaining a first option over all future production from a proposed scandium mine near Port Macquarie, New South Wales.
The interest shown by Ashurst, the largest known miner and consumer of scandium, an alloy metal, was a significant first step for Jervois, Pursell told Reuters.

Scandium is used sparingly in manufacturing metal hallogen lighting and other high-intensity lighting and fetchs up to A$680 an ounce. "In small quantities it is more valuable than gold," Pursell said. Gold now fetches about A$450 an ounce.
"The problem is that the new uses need an awful lot more scandium and of course the price can't stay that high," he said.
"You wouldn't be able to sell the alloys if you had to pay A$680 an ounce," Pursell said.

Introduction of a supply source the size of the Port Macquarie deposit -- estimated to hold nine million tonnes of ore, grading 36 grammes of scandium, eight kilograms of nickel and 1.1 kilogrammes of cobalt -- would go a long way in bringing down the price, Pursell said.
He said the mine was currently being studied as a source for nickel and cobalt, with scandium mined simply as a by-product, although that could change depending on future demand for scandium.
At peak levels, the mine would produce about 40 tonnes of scandium annually, he said.
"Anything from A$2 a gramme upwards would be a huge play for us ... it would make it a scandium mine with by product nickel and cobalt," Pursell said.
Jervois has been told by Ashurst that it is working with several aluminium companies and other end users of scandium to license the technology and build markets in partnership.

"In our estimation, that fact that (Jervois) will have substantial quantities of scandium available within the next three years coincides with our timing to substantially increase the volume of fine alloy," Ashurst said in a letter to Jervois, which was released by the Australian Stock Exchange.
Ashurst said it was confident the market could move from millions of pounds to hundreds of millions of pounds in the next two to five years.

"Encouraging results with our automotive partners indicate that performance can be achieved and now we must prove that the higher price of scandium would warrant a substantial integration of aluminium/scandium alloys in automotive structures," Ashurst said.
So-called specialist alloys are are finding end uses in the aerospace, sports equipment and marine indistries, as well as automotive, Pursell said.
Ashurst, formerly Emtech Ltd, is listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange, on the London AIM market, and is traded over-the-counter (OTC) in New York.
